intro: The Mahabharata is often called the longest poem in the world. It tells of two branches of one royal family, the five Pandava brothers and their hundred Kaurava cousins, and the great war between them.

Inside the Mahabharata is the Bhagavad Gita, a conversation between the warrior Arjuna and Krishna, his charioteer. Many Hindus treasure it as one of their most important texts. The epic also holds many smaller stories, like Savitri and Nala.

By the end, you will be able to name the main people and events of the epic. You will be able to explain Krishna's key teaching in Gita 2.47. You will be able to show how different readers answer the epic's hard questions.
bigQuestion: What does the Mahabharata teach about doing what is right when every choice is hard?

title: The Mahabharata and the Gita

chapters.title: Two Families, One Kingdom
chapters.bigQuestion: How do you decide what is right when everyone has a reason?

story.title: One Afternoon of Dice
story.kicker: A game of dice goes wrong, and a family loses its kingdom in one afternoon.
paragraphs: The great hall of Hastinapura glitters with gold. Kings and elders sit in rows along the walls. In the middle, two men kneel across from each other on a carpet. Between them lie a board and a pair of dice.

One of the players is Yudhishthira, the eldest of five brothers called the Pandavas. He is known for always telling the truth. The other side is led by his cousin Duryodhana, who is jealous of the Pandavas' new kingdom.
The dice roll. Yudhishthira loses a bag of jewels. The dice roll again. He loses his chariots. He keeps playing, hoping to win it all back. He loses his army. He loses his kingdom.
The elders shift in their seats. Some whisper that the game is unfair. No one stops it. By the end of the afternoon, Yudhishthira has lost everything, even his brothers and himself.
That one afternoon will lead to exile, anger and, years later, a terrible war. The Mahabharata asks its readers to think hard about who was right and who was wrong.
story.think: Why do you think no one stopped the game? What might you have done?

lessons.title: One of the Longest Poems
lessons.mainIdea: The Mahabharata is often called the longest poem in the world.
reading: The *Mahabharata* is an epic poem in Sanskrit. Its name means something like "the great story of the Bharata family." It is often called the longest poem in the world.
Its longest versions have about 100,000 verses. That is about seven times as long as the Iliad and the Odyssey of ancient Greece put together. It is divided into 18 books, called parvas.
The Mahabharata holds a huge family story. Inside it are many smaller stories, teachings and debates. One of them is the Bhagavad Gita, which you will study in the next chapter.

words.d: the great Sanskrit epic of the Bharata family and their war
one of the 18 books of the Mahabharata

lessons.title: Vyasa and Ganesha the Scribe
lessons.mainIdea: Tradition credits Vyasa with the Mahabharata, and a famous legend says Ganesha wrote it down.
reading: Hindu tradition says the sage *Vyasa* made the Mahabharata. Vyasa is also a character in the story. He is the grandfather of both the Pandavas and their cousins, the Kauravas.
A famous legend, found in some versions of the first book, tells how the poem was written down. Vyasa needed a scribe. Ganesha agreed, but only if Vyasa never stopped speaking.
Vyasa agreed, with one condition of his own: Ganesha must understand every verse before writing it. When Vyasa needed a rest, he spoke a very hard verse. Ganesha had to stop and think.

words.d: the sage whom tradition credits with the Mahabharata
a person who writes down or copies texts

look.title: A Clever Deal
look.text: Ganesha writes as fast as Vyasa can speak. The rule is: no stopping. But Vyasa has a plan. Whenever he needs a moment, he speaks a verse so tricky that Ganesha must pause to work it out.
look.prompt: What does this legend suggest about how hard some parts of the Mahabharata are?

lessons.title: When Was It Made?
lessons.mainIdea: Tradition and scholars give different dates for the Mahabharata.
reading: Hindu tradition places the Mahabharata war at the end of an ancient age called the Dvapara Yuga. Many Hindus believe the events happened thousands of years ago.
Scholars look at the poem's language and history. Most think it grew over many centuries, roughly between 400 BCE and 400 CE. Many storytellers added to it over time.
A fair student can name both views. You might say, "Tradition places the war in the Dvapara Yuga. Scholars think the poem grew between about 400 BCE and 400 CE."

words.d: in Hindu tradition, one of four great ages of the world
a period of 100 years

look.title: A Poem That Grew
look.text: Imagine a family story told for 800 years. Each teller adds a new detail or a lesson. A cousin adds a side story. A teacher adds a speech. By the end, the story is enormous. Scholars think the Mahabharata grew something like this.
look.prompt: Why might a story grow longer each time it is told?

lessons.title: The Five Pandavas
lessons.mainIdea: The five Pandava brothers are the heroes of the Mahabharata.
reading: The *Pandavas* are five brothers, the sons of King Pandu. Each one is known for a special quality. Their mother Kunti and stepmother Madri raise them.
Yudhishthira, the eldest, is known for truth and dharma. Bhima is famous for great strength. Arjuna is the best archer. The twins, Nakula and Sahadeva, are known for skill and wisdom.
The brothers are close and loyal. Many Hindus see them as heroes who try to live by dharma. But the epic also shows their mistakes, which makes the story richer.

words.d: the five sons of King Pandu, heroes of the Mahabharata
a person who shoots with a bow and arrows

lessons.title: The Hundred Kauravas
lessons.mainIdea: The Kauravas are the Pandavas' hundred cousins, led by Duryodhana.
reading: The *Kauravas* are the hundred sons of King Dhritarashtra, who is blind. They are cousins of the Pandavas. The eldest Kaurava is Duryodhana. He wants the throne for himself.
Duryodhana is jealous of the Pandavas. He believes the kingdom should belong to him and his brothers. He tries many times to get rid of his cousins. None of his plans succeed.
The epic does not make Duryodhana simple. He is also brave and loyal to his friends. Some readers feel he had real reasons to feel wronged, even if his actions were wrong.

words.d: the hundred sons of King Dhritarashtra, cousins of the Pandavas

look.title: Two Sides of Duryodhana
look.text: Duryodhana plots against his cousins. He cheats at dice. But he also stands by his friend Karna when others insult him. He fights bravely to the end. The Mahabharata shows him as more than just a villain.

lessons.title: Draupadi
lessons.mainIdea: Draupadi, the Pandavas' wife, is one of the strongest voices in the epic.
reading: *Draupadi* is a princess who becomes the wife of the five Pandava brothers. She is proud, clever and brave. Many readers see her as one of the strongest characters in the Mahabharata.
Draupadi speaks her mind. She asks hard questions of kings and elders. When she is treated unjustly, she demands that the wrong be put right. Her words shake the whole court.
Many Hindus honor Draupadi. In parts of South India, she is worshiped as a goddess in her own temples. Writers today still retell the epic from her point of view.

words.d: the princess who is the wife of the five Pandavas
fair treatment; making a wrong right

lessons.title: The Dice Game
lessons.mainIdea: In a rigged dice game, Yudhishthira loses everything, and Draupadi is shamed in the hall.
reading: The Sabha Parva, the book of the assembly hall, tells of the dice game. Duryodhana's uncle Shakuni plays for him. Many tellings say Shakuni's dice are loaded or his play is tricky.
Yudhishthira keeps betting and losing. He loses his wealth, his kingdom, his brothers, himself and finally Draupadi. She is dragged into the hall and insulted.
Draupadi asks the elders a sharp question: could a man who had already lost himself still bet her? No one gives a clear answer. Many tellings say Krishna protected her honor in the hall.

words.d: the book of the Mahabharata that tells of the dice game

lessons.title: Years in Exile
lessons.mainIdea: The Pandavas spend twelve years in the forest and one year in disguise.
reading: After the dice game, a second game is played. The Pandavas lose again. Now they must live in the forest for twelve years, then spend one more year hidden in disguise.
If they are found in the thirteenth year, they must start all over again. So they disguise themselves and serve in the court of King Virata. Arjuna even works as a dance teacher.
During the forest years, the Pandavas meet sages and hear many stories. Some of the best-loved stories inside the Mahabharata are told during this exile.

lessons.title: The War at Kurukshetra
lessons.mainIdea: When peace talks fail, the cousins fight an eighteen-day war at Kurukshetra.
reading: After thirteen years, the Pandavas ask for their kingdom back. Duryodhana refuses. They ask for just five villages. He refuses again. Krishna tries to make peace, but the talks fail.
The two sides meet on the plain of *Kurukshetra*. The poem says the war lasts eighteen days. Teachers, uncles and cousins face each other. Huge numbers die on both sides.
The Pandavas win, but the victory feels empty. So many loved ones are gone. Many readers see the Mahabharata as a story about the terrible cost of war.

words.d: the plain where the Mahabharata war is fought

lessons.title: Everyone Has a Reason
lessons.mainIdea: The Mahabharata shows hard choices where many people have reasons for what they do.
reading: Karna is one of the saddest figures in the epic. He is secretly the Pandavas' older brother, but he was raised by a charioteer's family. Duryodhana befriended him when others looked down on him.
Before the war, Karna learns the truth. He could join the Pandavas. But he stays loyal to Duryodhana, who stood by him. He fights against his own brothers.
Was Karna right or wrong? Readers disagree. The epic itself says that dharma is subtle, which means hard to see clearly. That is one reason people still argue about this story.

words.d: a great warrior, secretly the Pandavas' brother, who fights for Duryodhana
hard to see or understand clearly

look.title: Karna's Choice
look.text: Karna has two loyalties. One is to his true brothers, the Pandavas. The other is to his friend Duryodhana, who stood by him when no one else did. He cannot keep both.

chapters.title: Arjuna's Question and Stories Inside the Story
chapters.bigQuestion: What should you do when your duty feels too hard?

story.title: Following Death
story.kicker: A bride walks behind Death himself and will not stop asking.
paragraphs: Deep in a forest, a young woman named Savitri sits under a tree. Her husband, Satyavan, rests his head in her lap. He has been cutting wood all morning. Now he is very still.
A tall figure in dark red appears among the trees. He carries a noose. It is Yama, the lord of death. He has come for Satyavan's life, and he turns to leave.
Savitri stands up and follows him. Yama tells her to go home. She keeps walking. She speaks to him calmly and wisely about goodness and friendship. Yama is surprised.
Yama is pleased by her words. He offers her a wish, anything except her husband's life. She asks for something else. He offers another wish. She keeps following and keeps speaking.
At last, Savitri asks for a wish that Yama cannot grant unless Satyavan lives. Yama smiles and gives her husband back. This story is one of many stories told inside the Mahabharata.
story.think: Savitri did not fight Death. How did she win?

lessons.title: The Song of the Lord
lessons.mainIdea: The Bhagavad Gita is an 18-chapter teaching inside the Mahabharata.
reading: The *Bhagavad Gita* means "the song of the Lord." It is found in the sixth book of the Mahabharata, the Bhishma Parva. It has 18 chapters and 700 verses.
The whole Gita is a conversation. It takes place on the battlefield of Kurukshetra, just before the war begins. Arjuna asks questions, and Krishna answers them.
Many Hindus treasure the Gita above almost any other text. It has been translated into English and hundreds of other languages. Many families keep a copy at their home shrine.

words.d: "the song of the Lord"; Krishna's teaching to Arjuna in the Mahabharata
a talk between two or more people

lessons.title: Arjuna Puts Down His Bow
lessons.mainIdea: Arjuna does not want to fight his own relatives and teachers.
reading: Arjuna rides into the middle of the battlefield. He looks at the other army. He sees his uncles, his cousins, his friends and his beloved teacher, Drona.
Arjuna's body shakes. His mouth goes dry. He tells Krishna he does not want a kingdom if it means killing his own family. He sets down his bow and sits in the chariot.
The first chapter of the Gita is sometimes called "Arjuna's sorrow." Many readers see Arjuna's pain as very human. Anyone can feel stuck when every choice seems wrong.

words.d: the Pandava archer whom Krishna teaches in the Gita
deep sadness

look.title: Arjuna Cannot Fight

lessons.title: Krishna the Charioteer
lessons.mainIdea: Krishna, Arjuna's charioteer, becomes his teacher, and many Hindus honor him as God.
reading: In the Mahabharata, Krishna is Arjuna's friend and cousin. He agrees not to fight in the war. Instead, he drives Arjuna's chariot. A charioteer steers the horses.
When Arjuna sits down in despair, Krishna becomes his teacher. Later in the Gita, Krishna says he is God. Many Hindus honor Krishna as an avatar of Vishnu, or as God himself.
Many Hindu pictures show this scene. Krishna holds the reins of white horses and turns to speak. Arjuna listens with his hands folded. Families often hang this picture at home.

words.d: the person who drives a chariot
a form in which, Hindus believe, a deity comes into the world

look.prompt: Why might a teacher be shown as a driver in this story?

lessons.title: Do Your Duty, Not for the Reward
lessons.mainIdea: Krishna teaches Arjuna to do his duty without being greedy for the reward.
reading: One of the most famous verses in the Gita is 2.47. In it, Krishna says Arjuna has a right to his work, but not to its results. He should act without clinging to the reward.
Think of a student who studies hard because learning matters, not only for a prize. Many Hindus read this verse as advice to do good work and let go of worry about results.
Krishna calls this *karma yoga*, the path of action. Karma means action. In this path, a person does their duty well and offers the results to God, as many Hindus understand it.

words.d: action; also the idea that actions bring results
in the Gita, the path of doing your duty without clinging to the reward

look.title: Bhagavad Gita 2.47
look.text: Krishna tells Arjuna: your right is to your work, never to its fruits. Do not work only for the reward, and do not give up doing your work.
look.cite: Bhagavad Gita 2.47, retold from K. T. Telang's translation, Sacred Books of the East 8 (1882)

check.why: Gita 2.47 says to act without clinging to results.

check.why: Karma means action.

check.q: What is karma yoga?
choices: The path of action done without clinging to reward
check.why: In the Gita, karma yoga is selfless action.

lessons.title: The Self That Does Not Die
lessons.mainIdea: Krishna teaches that the true self, the atman, is never born and never dies.
reading: Krishna tells Arjuna not to grieve. He teaches that the true self, the *atman*, is not the body. The body is born and dies, but, the Gita says, the atman does not.
The Gita compares this to changing clothes. As a person throws away worn-out clothes and puts on new ones, the self leaves one body and takes on another (Gita 2.22).
This idea of being born again and again is called *samsara*. Many Hindus believe in samsara. Other religions have different beliefs about what happens after death.

words.d: the true self inside each being
the cycle of birth, death and rebirth

look.title: Like Changing Clothes
look.text: As a person throws off old, worn clothes and puts on new ones, the Gita says, the self leaves old bodies and enters new ones.
look.cite: Bhagavad Gita 2.22, retold from K. T. Telang's translation, Sacred Books of the East 8 (1882)

check.why: Gita 2.22 compares bodies to clothes that are changed.

check.q: What is samsara?

lessons.title: Many Ways to Read the Gita
lessons.mainIdea: Hindus and others read the Gita in many different ways.
reading: The Gita describes several paths. One is the path of action. One is the path of knowledge. One is *bhakti*, the path of loving devotion to God. Many Hindus say the Gita honors all three.
Readers also disagree about the battle. Some read it as a real war and a lesson about duty. Mahatma Gandhi read the battle as a picture of the struggle between good and bad inside each person.
Great Hindu teachers wrote commentaries on the Gita, explaining it in different ways. Today, families, students and leaders around the world still read it and argue about its meaning.

words.d: loving devotion to God

lessons.title: Savitri and Satyavan
lessons.mainIdea: Savitri chooses Satyavan as her husband, even though she knows he will die soon.
reading: During the Pandavas' forest exile, a sage tells them many stories. One is about Princess *Savitri*. She chooses a young man named Satyavan to marry. He lives in the forest with his blind father.
A sage warns her that Satyavan will die in exactly one year. Savitri says she has chosen and will not change her mind. She marries him and lives simply in the forest.
As the day draws near, Savitri fasts and prays. On the last day, she goes with Satyavan into the woods. This is where Yama, the lord of death, comes for him.

words.d: the princess in the Mahabharata who wins her husband back from Death
to go without food for a time, often for a religious reason

look.title: A Brave Choice

lessons.title: Savitri Wins
lessons.mainIdea: With patience and wise words, Savitri wins Satyavan back from Yama.
reading: When Yama takes Satyavan's life, Savitri follows him. She speaks wisely about goodness and friendship. Yama is pleased and grants her wishes, but never her husband's life.
She asks for her father-in-law's sight and kingdom to be restored. Then she asks to have many children with Satyavan. Yama agrees without thinking. But that wish needs Satyavan alive!
Yama keeps his word and returns Satyavan's life. Many Hindu women honor Savitri with a yearly fast and prayers for their families. The story is in the Vana Parva.

words.d: the lord of death in Hindu stories
staying calm and steady while you wait or work

look.title: The Last Wish
look.text: Savitri asks Yama for many sons with Satyavan. Yama grants it. Then she points out that the wish cannot come true unless her husband lives. Yama releases Satyavan.
look.cite: Retold from the Mahabharata, Vana Parva (Book 3); see K. M. Ganguli's translation (1883–96)
look.prompt: How did Savitri use Yama's own promise to win?

check.why: The Savitri story is in the Vana Parva, the forest book.

lessons.title: Nala and Damayanti
lessons.mainIdea: Nala and Damayanti lose everything through dice, and their love and courage bring them back together.
reading: Another forest story is about King *Nala* and Queen Damayanti. Nala loses his kingdom to his brother in a game of dice, much like Yudhishthira. Both kings lose everything.
Nala and Damayanti are separated in the forest. Damayanti searches bravely for her husband. Nala, changed in form, works as a charioteer for another king.
In the end, Damayanti finds a clever way to bring Nala back. He wins back his kingdom. The story is told to Yudhishthira to give him hope during his own exile.

words.d: a king in a Mahabharata story who loses his kingdom at dice and wins it back
the feeling that good things can still happen

lessons.title: "What Is Here Is Everywhere"
lessons.mainIdea: The Mahabharata claims to contain everything, and many readers find their own lives in it.
reading: The Mahabharata makes a bold claim about itself. It says that what is found in it may be found elsewhere, but what is not found in it is found nowhere.
The epic holds family quarrels, friendship, love, war, grief, and questions about right and wrong. Many readers say they recognize their own lives in its stories.
The Mahabharata has been retold as TV shows, plays, novels and comics. In 1985, the director Peter Brook staged a famous version that ran for about nine hours. People keep finding new meanings in it.

words.d: a statement that something is true
a very long poem about heroes and great deeds
